column4: In the comparison of hardened hearts, some stones split and water comes out, while others give rise to rivers. Its own contribution is water emerging from cleft ground, a specific parallel to the hidden water reached at the well.

Joseph is actually placed in the dark recess of the well, and God gives him a future assurance there. Unlike 12:10's proposal and 12:19's drawing of the bucket, this ayah contributes the lived depth of the well scene.

Neighbouring plots contain gardens, crops, and palms, all watered with one water while their fruit differs. It makes one sustaining water produce diverse living growth, closely extending the section's cloud-to-plant image.
Thunder gives praise to God while 13:12 has just raised the heavy clouds. This ayah's own contribution is praise within the storm, joining the H-M-D layer of the source to its cloud scene.
Destroyed settlements leave behind an abandoned well alongside a lofty palace. The unused well is a direct contrary image to the full, life-supporting wellhead in the section.

By the water settled in the earth in 23:18, God produces gardens of palms and vines with abundant fruit. This ayah supplies the cultivated plant result of the preceding measured rain and ground-water.

The livestock provide drink, benefit, and food after the water-and-garden sequence of 23:18–19. It concerns animal drink rather than well-water, but specifically extends the image's water-supported provision to herd life.

Every living creature is created from water, then shown moving in diverse ways. This repeats water's life-bearing role with particular attention to animal life, a secondary counterpart to the source's pasture and livestock.
Before the rain described in 30:48, people were in despair. Its own contribution is the human condition that the rain reverses, matching the source's account of rain repairing a people's state.
After the nearby rain-and-revival sequence, a sent wind leaves the visible growth yellow. It reverses the source's moist growth-bearing wind and fresh green earth.
Saba has two fruitful gardens and is told to eat its Lord's provision; 34:16 then names the flood that replaces them. This ayah contributes the settled fertile land before its water-related reversal.
The flood of the dam is sent and the two gardens are replaced by bitter fruit and sparse trees. It is a specific destructive reversal of water-fed abundance and tender vegetation.
The messenger warns his people to leave God's she-camel and its drinking. It adds a prophetic command about an animal's rightful water access to the water-share scenes in 26:155 and 54:28.
